messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 43

Carlos sits in the chair, a tall, broad-shouldered man with graying hair and a steady gaze that wavers only when he talks about the explosion. He is fifty-eight, married for thirty-two years to Marta, a high school principal. For the past twenty years he has worked as a forensic analyst for the city’s crime lab, specializing in fire and explosion scenes. He used to love the puzzle of it—the careful reconstruction of destruction. That was before.

The disaster happened three years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. Carlos was at the lab when a call came in: a warehouse fire in an industrial district, suspected arson. The building had housed a recycling plant that illegally stored volatile chemicals. He arrived with the investigation team two hours after the fire had been contained. The air still stung with burnt plastic and metal. He remembers the crackling sound of his own boots on melted asphalt, the way the corrugated roof had folded inward like a collapsed lung.

Then came the second explosion. No one had warned them about undetonated propane tanks in the basement. Carlos was about forty feet from the building when it happened—a wall of heat and debris that threw him into a parked van. He remembers the ringing in his ears, the taste of dust and blood, the sight of a colleague’s arm lying separate from his body. Four people died that day: two firefighters and two fellow analysts.

Carlos survived with a broken collarbone, torn ligaments in his knee, and a concussion. But the real damage didn’t show up on any scan. For weeks afterward, he couldn’t walk past a construction site without his chest tightening. He flinched at the sound of a car backfiring. Sleep became a battlefield. He would lie beside Marta, staring at the ceiling, afraid that if he closed his eyes he would see the arm again, the fire, the face of his friend Diego before it was gone.

He stopped going to the lab for six months. The department gave him leave, then light duty. When he finally returned, he couldn’t handle the evidence files from the same type of cases—any fire, any explosion. He asked to be reassigned to cold-case document review. His supervisors agreed, but the change felt like a shrinking. He used to teach seminars on fire scene reconstruction; now he sits in a cubicle scanning old reports, avoiding photographs of burned buildings.

Marta notices everything. She tells him he looks tired, that he seems distant. He knows she’s right. He has stopped going to his Sunday soccer games with friends. The noise of the crowd, the sudden shouts—it all feels too much. He drives the long way home to avoid a block where construction crews are using jackhammers. Sometimes, when he smells smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue, he freezes, his throat tight, his mind blank except for the image of that collapsing roof.

He does not believe he is traumatized. He tells himself he’s just getting older, that his body is slower, that any man would feel jumpy after nearly dying. But the PCL-5 score from the intake interview—a 43—suggests otherwise. That score comes from questions he answered carefully: the nightmares that still come twice a week, the way he avoids looking up old photos of Diego, the anger that flares when Marta asks him if he wants to talk about it.

He has not told her about the flashback that happened last week. He was at the grocery store, waiting in line, when a child dropped a glass jar. The shattering sound was exactly like the sound of a window breaking in the explosion. He dropped his basket, his heart pounding, his hands shaking. He left the store without buying anything. He sat in his car for ten minutes, breathing the way the online videos taught him—in through the nose, out through the mouth. It helped, but only until he got home. Then he sat in the garage, staring at the wall, until Marta came out to find him.

He wants to believe it will fade with time. But time, he is learning, is not a healer. It is a container. And the explosion is still inside it, waiting.
